subject: run calculateWAIC in a loop and only compile once

messages.author: e10074edba72b727
messages.subject: run calculateWAIC in a loop and only compile once
parts:
Hello,

I am running calculateWAIC on subsamples of a single model's output samples in a loop.  This is working, but in each step of the loop calculateWAIC recompiles a sub function, and I have run into the "maximal number of DLLs reached" error documented here: https://groups.google.com/g/nimble-users/c/-eoYs__eg0o.

I attempted to rewrite the calculateWAIC function as follows to get around the multiple compiles:

this function returns the compiled object (cwaicFun)

my.waic<-function (mcmc, model, nburnin = 0, thin = 1)
 ## running on a matrix, not mcmc object..
    if (!(is.matrix(mcmc) || is.data.frame(mcmc)))
      stop("calculateWAIC: 'mcmc' must be a matrix/dataframe of samples or a nimble MCMC object.")
    if (is.data.frame(mcmc))
      mcmc <- as.matrix(mcmc)
    if (missing(model))
      stop("calculateWAIC: 'model' is required if samples are directly provided rather than an MCMC object.")
    if (exists("Rmodel", model, inherits = FALSE))
      model <- model$Rmodel
    nm <- model$getVarNames(nodes = colnames(mcmc))
    modelSymbolObjects = model$getSymbolTable()$getSymbolObjects()
    if (!all(nm %in% names(modelSymbolObjects)))
      stop("calculateWAIC: some column names indicate variables that are not in the model.")
    mvSamplesConf <- modelValuesConf(nimble:::symbolTable(symbols = modelSymbolObjects[nm]))
    mvSamples <- modelValues(mvSamplesConf)
    usingMCMC <- FALSE

  waicFun <- nimble:::buildOfflineWAIC(model, mvSamples, NULL, mvSamples$varNames)
  cwaicFun <- compileNimble(waicFun, project = model, resetFunctions = TRUE)
  # if (!usingMCMC) {
  #   matrix2mv(mcmc, cwaicFun$mvSamples)
  # }
  # else matrix2mv(samples, cwaicFun$mvSamples)
  # messageIfVerbose("Calculating WAIC.")
  # result <- cwaicFun$calculateWAIC(nburnin, thin)
  # return(result)
  return(cwaicFun)
}

then I tried to use the compiled fn returned above to calculate waic on subsamples:

c.waic.fun <- my.waic(mcmc = samples$samples , model =  c.run.model, nburnin = 0, thin = 1)

subsamples = some subset of samples$samples (samples$samples[c(2000:3000),]

## attempt to get waic
nimble:::matrix2mv(subsamples, c.waic.fun$mvSamples)
result <- c.waic.fun$calculateWAIC(nburnin=0, thin=1)

this calculates a waic value, but it does not match the waic if I run:
calculateWAIC(mcmc = subsamples, model = c.run.model, nburnin = 0, thin = 1)

so.. clearly i do not fully understand what is going on under the hood here. Maybe the subfunction (nimble:::buildOfflineWAIC) could be rewritten with a setup and run fn to be compiled with the current model, then run on a set of samples? or maybe I am missing something simple..

I would be grateful for any advice,

Thank you,
Brian

messages.author: d78486bfff620d81
messages.subject: Re: run calculateWAIC in a loop and only compile once
parts:
Hi Brian,

A few thoughts, though I think #1 may be enough.

1) When you run `my.waic`, I think you need to pass in one of the subsamples matrices not the full matrix. That looks like it works when I try it. Otherwise, you might be calculating WAIC on a bunch of rows with zeros or some such (I haven't looked closely).
2) You can unload DLLs, as described here in the manual. That may be a quick and dirty fix.
3) A more comprehensive approach might work as follows. This would involve a deeper dive into the code but if you wanted to do this sort of thing a lot, it might be worth it. The buildWAIC nimblefunction has a `reset` function that resets the summary statistics used in calculating WAIC. I think you can make use of that in combination with setting `lengthConvCheck` to be equal to the number of subsets you want. Then, every X iterations, in the `updateStats` method you can save the current WAIC and reset the summary stats. Note that the ability to have the `WAIC`, `lppd`, `pWAIC` storage objects have length greater than one is intended for assessing Monte Carlo uncertainty when using marginal WAIC, but I think you can repurpose things.

-chris
